analysis.one_liner: Removes the insurance industry's exemption from antitrust laws against price fixing and monopolies.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: it sat in the Senate Judiciary Committee from October 1991 until Congress ended in January 1993.
analysis.plain_summary: Since 1945, the McCarran-Ferguson Act has shielded the insurance business from most federal antitrust laws. This bill would strip that shield for the worst conduct: price fixing, dividing up markets with competitors, forcing customers to buy one product to get another, and monopolizing. It would keep the shield for innocuous sharing of historical loss data and actuarial work, so insurers could still pool statistics to price policies. The bill never received a hearing, a vote, or any committee action.
analysis.who_benefits: Insurance customers. With federal antitrust laws applicable, insurers could no longer fix prices, carve up territories, or monopolize lines of insurance without facing enforcement, which would put competitive pressure on premiums.

how_it_helps.text: The bill amends the McCarran-Ferguson Act so that price fixing, market allocation, unlawful tying, and monopolization in the insurance business are no longer shielded from federal antitrust law, including FTC Act restraints-of-trade provisions.

It preserves the exemption for collecting and sharing historical loss data, computing loss development factors, and performing actuarial services, so insurers can still pool the statistics needed to price policies accurately.
The bill would take effect one year after enactment, giving the industry time to adjust.

analysis.who_pays: Insurance companies, which would lose their decades-old protection from federal antitrust enforcement for anticompetitive conduct, and would face potential lawsuits and government enforcement.

drawbacks.text: State insurance regulators argued that state regulation of insurance would be complicated by overlapping federal antitrust enforcement, and insurers contended the exemption was needed to allow data sharing and joint rate-setting in fragmented markets. The bill tries to address the data-sharing concern with an express carve-out for actuarial work and loss statistics.
Enforcement costs and litigation over what counts as unlawful tying or monopolization would fall partly on insurers and could be passed to policyholders in the short run.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The consumer case is straightforward: competition generally lowers prices, and insurance was uniquely exempt from the laws that apply to nearly every other industry. The bill was drafted narrowly, targeting only the clearest anticompetitive conduct and protecting legitimate statistical cooperation, so the main genuine cost is added legal complexity for an industry that was already regulated by the states.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee in October 1991, and the committee never took it up before the 102nd Congress ended in January 1993.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on October 24, 1991 by Senator Metzenbaum, joined by Senators Simon, Biden, and Kennedy.
It was read twice and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee the same day.
The action history shows no further action: no hearing, no committee vote, no floor consideration before the 102nd Congress ended on January 3, 1993.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Insurance companies are better off, because they kept the McCarran-Ferguson antitrust exemption the bill would have removed, and policyholders continue to buy insurance in a market insulated from federal antitrust enforcement.

for.name: Howard M. Metzenbaum
for.role: U.S. Senator (D-OH); bill sponsor and longtime critic of the insurance antitrust exemption
for.what_they_did: Introduced S. 1873 on October 24, 1991 to strip the McCarran-Ferguson exemption for price fixing and monopolization in insurance.

for.name: Paul Simon, Joseph Biden, and Edward Kennedy
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill as its only additional Senate supporters.

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on October 24, 1991 and took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — before the Congress ended.

against.name: Insurance industry groups
against.what_they_did: Long opposed narrowing the McCarran-Ferguson antitrust exemption, which shielded insurance rate-setting and market practices from federal antitrust enforcement.

sides.party_line_note: All four sponsors were Democrats, and no Republican support appears in the record; the bill's only obstacles were Democratic-held committee inaction rather than a recorded vote.

industries.note: The bill would end their exemption from federal antitrust laws for price fixing, market allocation, tying, and monopolization, exposing conduct that is currently lawful under the McCarran-Ferguson Act to enforcement. That protection has allowed coordinated rate-setting that keeps premiums higher than a fully competitive market would produce.

The bill expressly preserves cooperation on historical loss data, loss development factors, and actuarial services, so the statistical infrastructure of insurance pricing survives intact as long as it is not used to restrain trade.
